extracted.intended_audience: stakeholders and practitioners submitting public comments on Federal Reserve rulemakings (banks, trade associations, consumer advocates, academics, attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for finding Federal Reserve proposed rules and submitting effective public comments, including procedural instructions (how/where to submit, deadlines, disclosure) and substantive content elements that increase influence with the Board.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission methods and attachments
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments can be submitted through the Federal Reserve's web site using the "Submit Comment" links (the preferred method of submission). The submission form allows for attachments. Comments may also be submitted in writing or by electronic mail (see text of each proposal for contact information).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the web site's "Submit Comment" link as preferred; you may attach supporting documents. If choosing non-web methods, follow contact information in the proposal text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding and accessing proposed rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed regulations are published in the Federal Register, the daily journal of the U.S. government, and the Board also maintains a list of its proposed regulations on its website. You can find, review, and submit comments at Regulations.gov.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locate proposals via the Federal Register, the Fed's list of proposed regulations, or directly on Regulations.gov for review and submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comment period and deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed regulations typically ask for public comment by a specific date. Comment periods often are 60 days, but the period may be longer or shorter depending on the circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check each proposal for its specific deadline; do not assume a 60-day window in all cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public disclosure and confidentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments received are subject to public disclosure and in general, comments received will be made available without change and will not be modified to remove personal or business information including confidential, contact, or other identifying information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume submissions become public in full; avoid including confidential or identifying information unless you intend it to be public, or follow any guidance in the proposal for claiming confidential treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite specific Fed Regulations by part
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective Fed comments typically: Cite specific Fed Regulations (Reg B, Reg E, Reg Z, Reg CC, etc.) by part
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference the exact regulation and part number being affected rather than only high-level descriptions to make the comment actionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference governing statutes (Federal Reserve Act, FDIA, BHCA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective Fed comments typically: Reference Federal Reserve Act, FDIA, BHCA provisions
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tie your comments to the statutory authorities and constraints that govern the Board's rulemaking to strengthen legal and policy arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage with quantitative impact analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective Fed comments typically: Engage with quantitative impact analysis
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide or critique quantitative estimates of costs, benefits, incidence, or other measurable effects; include data or models where possible to support claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address safety and soundness implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective Fed comments typically: Address safety and soundness implications
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how the proposed rule would affect bank safety and soundness outcomes, including risk-taking, capital adequacy, and supervisory implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish impacts by bank size categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective Fed comments typically: Distinguish impacts on different bank size categories ($100M, $10B, $250B thresholds)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze and, where possible, quantify how effects differ across bank size thresholds specified by the Board; avoid one-size-fits-all assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider community bank relief
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective Fed comments typically: Address community bank relief considerations
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss disproportionate burdens on community banks and suggest tailored relief or scaling approaches if appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite empirical research on bank behavior and market impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective Fed comments typically: Cite empirical research on bank behavior, market impacts
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support assertions with peer-reviewed studies, working papers, or reputable empirical analyses that bear on likely behavioral or market responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference Basel and international harmonization
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective Fed comments typically: Reference Basel and international harmonization where relevant
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposals relate to capital, liquidity, or supervisory standards, discuss consistency with Basel or other international frameworks and implications for cross-border comparability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider macroprudential implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective Fed comments typically: Consider macroprudential implications
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate systemic effects, interactions with broader financial stability policies, and unintended aggregate outcomes beyond firm-level impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key substantive topic areas where comments influence rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Key Areas Where Fed Comments Influence Rules: Capital and liquidity rules (Basel III implementation); Stress testing and CCAR; Volcker Rule; Consumer compliance regulations (CRA, fair lending); Payment systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus comments on these substantive areas when relevant, as the Board frequently acts in these domains; tailor argumentation and evidence to the specific policy area.
